title: The Compton Cafeteria Riot
summary: Stuff You Should Know overlooked-history episode on the Compton's Cafeteria Riot, a August 1966 uprising at Compton's Cafeteria at 101 Taylor Street in San Francisco's Tenderloin, in which trans women, gay and street youth fought police after years of harassment. The hosts cover the Tenderloin's conditions, the Glide Memorial Methodist Church and Cecil Williams, the Vanguard group, the riot itself and its aftermath, how the event was forgotten (compared with Stonewall), historian Susan Striker's research and the documentary Screaming Queens, the National Transsexual Counseling Unit, and the later naming of the street and the Transgender Cultural District. The episode ends with listener mail from Danny about "handburgers" and knowledge gaps.

entities.name: Screaming Queens: The Riot at Compton's Cafeteria

segments.title: Opening and listener suggestion
segments.summary: Josh introduces the overlooked-history pick, suggested by listener GG Cowlin, and the hosts say the riot was nearly lost to history until Susan Striker pieced it together.

segments.title: Comparison to Stonewall
segments.summary: The hosts say the 1966 riot resembled Stonewall: a response to police harassment by a multiracial LGBTQ group that spilled into the streets, yet it was pushed out of history.

segments.title: The Tenderloin in the 1960s
segments.summary: The Tenderloin is described as a poor, transient neighborhood with drugs, gambling and sex work, where LGBTQ teenagers run out of home gathered for community. Police could arrest people for cross-dressing or even button placement on shirts.

segments.title: Lives of unhoused trans youth
segments.summary: Unhoused trans youths could not get gender-matching ID to work, were often pushed into sex work, and were confined to a few blocks of the Tenderloin where they were still harassed and beaten.

segments.title: Compton's Cafeteria
segments.summary: Compton's Cafeteria at 101 Taylor Street was a 24-hour local chain restaurant opened in 1954 by Gene Compton's family business, serving as a late-night gathering place, though the owners sometimes called police on patrons.

segments.title: Community and homophile groups
segments.summary: Trans patrons were excluded even from gay bars. Homophile groups such as the Mattachine Society sought respectability and excluded the street youth, who then organized themselves.

segments.title: Glide Church and Vanguard
segments.summary: Glide Memorial Methodist Church and Reverend Cecil Williams helped the youth form Vanguard in 1965, and the Tenderloin was recognized as a War on Poverty target district in May 1966.

segments.title: Rising tensions before the riot
segments.summary: Compton's began calling police on trans patrons more often as Vanguard organized, and Vanguard picketed outside the cafeteria about a month before the riot.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-roll break.

segments.title: Date and course of the riot
segments.summary: The riot is dated to late August 1966, likely August 27, a Saturday, after police became aggressive, a patron threw coffee at an officer, and fighting spread. Patrons broke windows and flipped tables, and about sixty people fought police, who later retreated and returned in force; a police car was destroyed and a newsstand set on fire.

segments.title: Aftermath at Compton's and the police
segments.summary: Compton's barred drag queen patrons and began closing at midnight; pickets followed. Police harassment of trans youth reportedly dropped afterward, and the riot energized the organizing community.

segments.title: Reforms and the National Transsexual Counseling Unit
segments.summary: Community relations officer Elliott Blackstone advocated ending anti-cross-dressing laws, and the Center for Special Problems helped with gender-matching IDs. The riot is credited with founding the National Transsexual Counseling Unit, an early support group offering housing leads, hormone guidance and a mail drop.

segments.title: Violent versus nonviolent protest
segments.summary: Hosts muse on a future episode about violent and nonviolent protest and mention a stat that nonviolent movements succeed more often than violent ones.

segments.title: Why the riot was forgotten
segments.summary: Few publications covered the riot. Raymond Broshears wrote about it in a 1972 Gay Pride program, and drag queen Sandy Green mentioned it in a letter to the editor around 1973. Reasons for the gap include New York's media dominance and the Stonewall-era shift toward activism.

segments.title: Why the community ignored it
segments.summary: The hosts suggest the riot clashed with the respectable image homophile groups wanted, so it was sidelined; only a couple of written mentions survived, which highlights Susan Striker's detective work.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-roll break.

segments.title: Susan Striker's research and the documentary
segments.summary: Striker, a trained historian transitioning to a woman in the early 1990s, found the 1972 program at the Gay and Lesbian Historical Society. City archives had destroyed police records, so she tracked down oral-history witnesses, and co-made the documentary Screaming Queens with Victor Silverman in 2005.

segments.title: Unsung History interview and newsreel
segments.summary: Striker discussed the research on the Unsung History podcast, with a geographer helping map the vanished area. An old newsreel described Compton's closing at midnight as a sidewalk catfight, with no police involved.

segments.title: Street renaming and Transgender Cultural District
segments.summary: The 2015 Group I hotel development sparked preservation fights. The city renamed the Taylor Street stretch Gene Compton's Cafeteria Way, then dropped the name. It is now a transgender cultural district, reportedly the first in the world, with housing and job support.

segments.title: Street name joke and game score
segments.summary: Hosts joke about naming a street Quiet Riot Boulevard, then Josh and Chuck trade points on the gullibility score.

segments.title: Listener mail: Danny and handburgers
segments.summary: Listener Danny says he started listening after a former partner belittled him for knowledge gaps, and he jokingly calls hamburgers handburgers. Josh and Chuck respond about IV and everyday knowledge gaps.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for listener mail and close with the iHeartRadio credit.
